sentence: Pancreatic cancer is a cancer that starts in the pancreas, an organ that helps with digestion.
note: Textbook: pancreas role in digestion; MedlinePlus page covers pancreatic cancer.

sentence: Pancreatic cancer often causes no symptoms at first, and when symptoms appear they can be vague.
note: MedlinePlus: early cancer often no symptoms, when they appear often vague. NHS: may have no symptoms or hard to spot.

sentence: The NHS says it can be difficult to treat.
note: NHS treatment summary: pancreatic cancer can be difficult to treat.

sentence: Known risk factors include smoking, long-term diabetes, chronic pancreatitis and certain hereditary disorders, although many people with risk factors never develop it.
note: MedlinePlus: risk factors listed; many with risk factors never develop it.

sentence: Treatment options include surgery, chemotherapy and radiotherapy, and when a cure is not possible the focus is on controlling symptoms.
note: MedlinePlus/NCI: surgery, radiation, chemotherapy, targeted therapy; palliative treatment to control symptoms when cure not possible.

sentence: Doctors do not know exactly what causes pancreatic cancer
note: MedlinePlus: doctors do not know what causes pancreatic cancer.

sentence: Risk factors such as smoking and long-term diabetes are linked to it, but many people with them never develop the cancer
note: MedlinePlus: many people with risk factors never develop it.

sentence: Smoking
note: MedlinePlus lists smoking; can be changed.

sentence: Long-term diabetes
Chronic pancreatitis

note: MedlinePlus: certain hereditary disorders, genetics and family history.

sentence: Being overweight or obese
note: Warrington PCN and Royal Marsden pages list overweight/obesity (search summary).

sentence: Older age, with one NHS source listing age over 65
note: Both NHS-affiliated pages list age over 65.

sentence: Yellowing of the skin and eyes (jaundice)
note: NHS: yellowing of skin or eyes common sign.

sentence: Weight loss without trying
note: NHS and CRUK list weight loss.

sentence: Changes to stools or bowel habits
note: CRUK: changes to stools; NHS: changes in bowel habits.

sentence: A blocked bile duct, causing jaundice
note: Macmillan: blocked bile ducts cause jaundice.

sentence: Reduced production of digestive enzymes, which can lead to malnutrition
note: NCI: removing part of pancreas can reduce enzymes; replacement prevents malnutrition. Applies after surgery; cancer itself also (trial text) - kept to NCI wording scope.

sentence: Spread of the cancer to other parts of the body
note: NCI: treatment options depend on whether cancer has spread; chemotherapy main treatment once spread.

sentence: Pain, tiredness and nausea
note: NHS: supportive care covers digestion problems, pain, tiredness and nausea.

sentence: Diagnosis typically combines a physical examination, blood tests, imaging and a biopsy, which is a sample of tissue.
note: MedlinePlus: physical exam, blood tests, imaging, biopsy. Definition of biopsy is textbook-level gloss.

sentence: Doctors use information from several tests, along with symptoms and medical history.
NICE guidance recommends a CT scan using a pancreatic protocol as the first scan for suspected pancreatic cancer.
note: NICE NG85 (via search): offer pancreatic protocol CT to people with jaundice (before bile duct drainage) and to those with abnormalities but no jaundice.

sentence: If the diagnosis is still unclear, a PET-CT scan, an endoscopic ultrasound or both may be offered.
note: NICE NG85: if unclear offer FDG-PET/CT and/or EUS.

sentence: Treatment depends on the size and position of the cancer, whether it has spread and the person's general health.
Surgery is used to remove the cancer when it can be removed, and to relieve symptoms such as jaundice or blockages when it cannot.
Chemotherapy and radiotherapy are also used, and targeted therapy is another option.
note: NHS: chemo and radiotherapy; MedlinePlus: surgery, radiation, chemo, targeted therapy.

sentence: Supportive and palliative care can help with symptoms such as pain, tiredness, nausea and digestion problems.
note: NHS supportive care; Macmillan palliative care.

sentence: Smoking is a risk factor that can be changed.
note: MedlinePlus: some risk factors like smoking can be changed.

sentence: Pancreatic Cancer UK says the UK has no screening programme, although people with a family history may be monitored.
note: Search summary of Pancreatic Cancer UK: no screening programme; people with family history may be monitored.

sentence: The NHS advises an urgent GP appointment or a call to NHS 111 for yellowing of the skin or eyes.
Pancreatic Cancer UK says jaundice needs a GP or A&E straight away.
note: Search summary of Pancreatic Cancer UK.

sentence: A GP appointment is advised for noticeable weight loss without trying or other symptoms that last longer than two weeks.
note: NHS summary: GP visit for noticeable weight loss or symptoms persisting beyond two weeks.

sentence: Having these symptoms does not definitely mean a person has pancreatic cancer.
note: NHS notes symptoms do not definitely mean pancreatic cancer.

sentence: The NHS says pancreatic cancer may not cause any symptoms, or the symptoms may be hard to spot.
MedlinePlus says early pancreatic cancer often does not cause symptoms right away, and that when symptoms appear they are often vague.
Yellowing of the skin or eyes, called jaundice, is one of the common signs.
The NHS also lists loss of appetite, losing weight without trying and tiredness.
Digestive symptoms include nausea and changes in bowel habits, and the NHS describes upper abdominal pain that may ease when leaning forward.
Cancer Research UK lists tummy or back pain and changes to stools among the common symptoms.
Pancreatic Cancer UK adds indigestion and recently diagnosed diabetes, while Macmillan also lists feeling very tired and feeling bloated after meals.
note: Summary attributes indigestion/new diabetes to Pancreatic Cancer UK; tired/bloated to Macmillan.

sentence: Many of these symptoms have other causes.
note: NHS and Pancreatic Cancer UK stress symptoms are common and often have other causes.

sentence: The NHS notes that having them does not definitely mean a person has pancreatic cancer.
MedlinePlus says doctors do not know what causes pancreatic cancer.
Known risk factors include smoking, long-term diabetes, chronic pancreatitis and certain hereditary disorders.
Some risk factors, such as smoking, can be changed, while others, such as genetics and family history, cannot.
Many people with risk factors never develop pancreatic cancer, while some people with no known risk factors do.
Other NHS-affiliated pages list being overweight or obese and being over 65 as factors that can raise the risk.
note: Warrington PCN and Royal Marsden search summaries.

sentence: The Royal Marsden page also lists heavy drinking and a high intake of red or processed meat.
Pancreatic Cancer UK says there is no screening programme for pancreatic cancer in the UK, although people with a family history may be monitored.
note: Search summary of Pancreatic Cancer UK.

sentence: MedlinePlus says diagnosis typically combines a physical examination, blood tests, imaging and a biopsy.
Doctors use information from several tests, together with the symptoms and medical history.
NICE guidance recommends a CT scan using a pancreatic protocol for people with suspected pancreatic cancer, including before the bile duct is drained in people with jaundice caused by a blockage.
If the diagnosis is still unclear, NICE says a PET-CT scan, an endoscopic ultrasound or both may be offered.
A published review describes endoscopic ultrasound with a fine-needle biopsy as the standard way of establishing the diagnosis.
note: PMC review snippet: EUS with fine-needle biopsy standard of care for establishing diagnosis.

sentence: A CT-guided biopsy can be an alternative when endoscopic ultrasound is unsuitable or unavailable, mainly for tumours that cannot be removed.
Cancer Research UK says a procedure called ERCP can help confirm the diagnosis by taking samples from abnormal areas.
The same procedure can be used to place a small tube, called a stent, in a blocked bile duct.
The NHS says pancreatic cancer can be difficult to treat.
The options depend on the size and position of the cancer, whether it has spread and the person's general health.
Surgery is used to remove the cancer when it can be removed, and also to relieve symptoms such as jaundice or blockages when it cannot.
The National Cancer Institute says surgery is only potentially curative when the tumour can be removed.
The National Cancer Institute describes chemotherapy as the main treatment once the cancer has spread, and says it can sometimes shrink the tumour or help people live longer.
The NHS lists chemotherapy and radiotherapy among the treatments used.
MedlinePlus also lists targeted therapy as an option.
For many people it will not be possible to cure pancreatic cancer.
note: Search summary text; source page not identified with certainty (Macmillan/NCI).

sentence: In those cases the main aim is often to control symptoms, and palliative treatment can improve quality of life by easing the symptoms and complications of the disease.
Macmillan says palliative care doctors and nurses specialise in symptom control and supportive care, and that a GP or specialist can refer a person to a palliative team.
The NHS says supportive care covers issues such as digestion problems, pain, tiredness and nausea.
The National Cancer Institute explains that removing part of the pancreas can reduce its ability to make digestive enzymes, so replacement enzymes may be prescribed to prevent malnutrition.
A blocked bile duct causes jaundice, and a stent can keep the duct open so that bile drains.
If a stent is not suitable, bypass surgery is an alternative, and medication can ease the itching that jaundice may cause.
For many people it will not be possible to cure pancreatic cancer, and the main aim of treatment is then often to control symptoms.
